sections.scenario: Riya rents a one-bedroom in Austin. Her laundry sits in a 60 in wide alcove. She can add shelves and a folding counter if they stay removable, but she cannot move plumbing, add a dryer vent through an exterior wall, or drill a load-bearing concrete wall without written permission.
sections.principle: Write the space, the machines, and the money before you buy a board.
body: This book is millwork around machines that already exist: a folding counter, shelves, and labeled storage. It is not a license to install a washer, dryer, gas line, new drain, or new dedicated circuit. Hire a licensed plumber or electrician for those. A renter usually may use freestanding or limited-fastener millwork if the lease and HOA or landlord rules allow it. An owner may fasten into suitable structure after checking services in the wall.

All prices in this book are US dollars (USD). The worked millwork envelope is $200 for sheet goods, lumber, fasteners, primer, paint, caulk, and consumables for one compact alcove. It does not include the washer or dryer, plumber or electrician fees, appliance delivery, stacking kits, or tools you already own. If you use the worksheet outside the United States, convert the $200 envelope and check local product names and sheet sizes.

Pick one construction level before you shop. No-drill: freestanding frames, tension poles only where the maker rates them, and nothing that depends on wall screws. Limited-fastener: a few screws into identified structure, with landlord permission, a removal plan, and a load you can actually support. Permanent: owner approval, and professional help if the wall, vent, or electrics are uncertain. Removable is not the same as renter-safe. A frame that can tip, overload hollow plaster, or block hose shutoffs is not a weekend win.

steps.text: Write one sentence: balcony utility, internal wet area, or dedicated laundry closet — and whether you rent or own.
Write the millwork envelope in USD and list what it excludes (machines, trades, tools).
Circle no-drill, limited-fastener, or permanent before you sketch shelves.

sections.mistake: Starting with a Pinterest shelf height, then discovering the lid on a top-load washer cannot open.

sections.title: Choose The Appliance Setup First

hero.query: Shopping aisle in a home improvement store with plywood and brackets, soft natural light, minimalist design, no people, no text, no watermark.

sections.principle: Shelf heights and counter spans follow the machines, not the other way around.
body: Select the appliance arrangement before you choose shelf heights, countertop dimensions, or support locations. Front-load washer: door swing, loading access, service clearance, and vibration. Top-load washer: lid opening height, overhead clearance, and access to controls. Stacked washer and dryer: only an approved stacking kit for those exact models, vertical load path, and service access to both units. Side-by-side machines: width, side clearance, shared folding surface, and both door swings. Washer only: leave a future dryer path if you might add one, plus hose and drain access.

A stacked pair is not a side-by-side pair with the dryer lifted. Stacking changes the load on the floor, the reach to the dryer door, and the service path. Do not invent a homemade shelf to carry a dryer unless that arrangement is specifically designed and approved for that purpose. Do not put a washer or dryer on an improvised countertop.

A French cleat is two interlocking strips, usually wood, cut at about 45 degrees: one on the wall, one on the furniture. A cleat (without “French”) is simply a strip the shelf sits on. You will use those words later. First, write which of the five setups you have.

steps.text: Circle one: front-load, top-load, stacked, side-by-side, or washer only.
If stacked, confirm a maker-approved stacking kit exists for both model numbers.
If top-load, measure lid arc before any overhead shelf height.

sections.mistake: Drawing a 36 inch counter over a top-load washer whose lid needs more than that to open.
checklist: Stacking kit confirmed or stacking rejected
No appliance sitting on improvised millwork

sections.title: Manufacturer Manuals Before Any Cut

hero.query: Close-up of custom shelves and countertop in a laundry alcove, soft natural light, minimalist design, no people, no text, no watermark.

sections.principle: Generic alcove numbers are planning starts. The installation manual is the rule.
body: Record washer and dryer make and model. Obtain the installation manuals. Record required rear, side, top, and front clearances. Confirm ventilation and exhaust requirements where a dryer is present. Confirm water inlet, drain, and electrical connection locations. Confirm the service and removal path. Check whether a stacking kit is approved for those exact models.

A shelf, countertop, or enclosure must not reduce required ventilation, access, or manufacturer-specified clearances. If the manual and this book disagree, follow the manual. If you cannot find the manual, stop millwork that sits within 4 inch of the machine until you have it.

Electrical modifications, new outlets, and uncertain wiring belong to a qualified electrician. Never run a washer or dryer on an unsuitable extension cord. Keep water connections and electrical components arranged to the applicable electrical safety rules — this book does not publish a generic outlet-clearance number for every jurisdiction.

steps.text: Photograph the model stickers and save the PDFs of both installation manuals.
Copy the maker's clearance table into your measurement sheet — do not invent substitutes.
Mark shutoff valves, drain, vent termination, and the plug so millwork cannot bury them.

sections.mistake: Building a pretty box that covers the shutoff, the lint path, or the plug.
checklist: Make, model, and manuals on the clipboard
Clearances copied from the maker, not from memory
Service path still open on the sketch

sections.scenario: Ravi’s Austin alcove is 48 in wide and 24 in deep to the plaster, but a drain box steals 3/4 in on the left. The walls are not square.
sections.principle: The smallest width, the shallowest depth, and the maker’s rear clearance govern the build.
body: Measure width at the floor, at mid-height, and near the top. Measure depth at left, center, and right. Measure height at the back and the front. Use the smallest width and the shallowest depth for cuts. Baseboards, tile lips, and hose boxes shrink the usable opening.

Hoses bulge. Walls bow. Doors swing. If you guess, you will cut shelves that jam at the baseboard and a counter that blocks the drain. Keep plumbing and electrical where they are unless a licensed trade is moving them.

Immediate function for most US apartment laundry closets is a folding surface you do not sit appliances on, two or three shelves, and labeled bins. That is the millwork envelope. It is not a full laundry-room renovation.
sections.mistake: Measuring only at chest height, then discovering the baseboard is 5/8 in thicker than the wall above.
checklist: Width, depth, and height recorded at multiple points
Smallest width and shallowest depth circled for cuts
No plumbing or electrical moves on the DIY list

sections.title: Moisture Suitability By Material

hero.query: Laundry alcove with adjustable shelving made from MDF, organized storage bins, and a clean countertop, natural light from one window, photorealistic.
hero.flux_prompt: A focused shot of the adjustable shelving in the laundry alcove, highlighting the materials used and organization.

sections.principle: No sheet good is universally right for a damp laundry alcove.
body: Plywood (typically 3/4 in for a folding counter, 1/2 in or 3/4 in for shelves): better moisture behavior than raw MDF if edges are sealed; still needs edge protection and a washable finish. Medium-density fibreboard (MDF): smooth for paint, cheaper, swells fast if edges stay raw — poor as an unsealed counter in a wet alcove. Melamine-faced board: wipeable face, vulnerable at every cut edge unless banded. Finish: bonding primer on every cut, then satin or semi-gloss enamel; add a water-based polyurethane on a folding counter if the product allows it over paint.

Shelves hold bottles and baskets. A folding counter is a work surface for laundry, not a stand for a washer or dryer unless the whole assembly is designed and approved for that load. Concentrated loads — a person leaning, a wet basket — matter more than a uniformly distributed textbook load.
Choose by moisture exposure, ventilation, the load, and how well you will seal edges. Skip exotic boards for a weekend envelope. Skip untreated particle board in the splash zone.
sections.mistake: Using raw MDF as a splash-zone counter because it was cheaper per sheet.
checklist: Shelf material written, with edge-seal method
No appliance load assigned to an improvised top

sections.scenario: Aditi’s Brooklyn wet area has a window on one side. She already chose a front-load washer with a ventless dryer stacked on a factory kit. Overhead shelves sit beside the stack, not over the dryer exhaust path — there is no exhaust duct, but the kit still needs the maker’s top clearance.
sections.principle: Zones follow doors, lids, vents, and shutoffs.
body: Put detergent within a short reach of the washer door or lid. Keep tall bottles where they cannot fall onto controls. Draw the door or lid arc on the sketch. Leave the shutoff valves, drain hose, and plug reachable without unscrewing millwork.

Vented dryers need a clear exhaust path; ventless dryers do not use that duct, but they still have maker clearances and lint access. Do not assume every US home has the same dryer type. A shelf near an exhaust route is allowed only if the installation instructions still work.
Bring the sketch to the home center. Do not cut to an example width from later chapters until this sketch matches your smallest measurements and the manuals.

Dryer type (vented, ventless, or none) written

sections.principle: Name the job of the top before you name the span.
body: Most readers in this book need a folding and sorting surface over or beside machines, supported on wall cleats or a freestanding frame. That is not the same as a structural shelf carrying a dryer. Do not support appliances on an improvised shelf or countertop unless the arrangement is specifically designed and approved for that purpose.

Identify the material, thickness, support spacing, and attachment method. A common US-available starting stack for a folding top is 3/4 in plywood, sealed edges, with cleats on the back and both sides where the walls and construction level allow. That stack is a starting description, not an engineered rating for every width.
The cut-list matrix later in the book is illustrative. Do not cut materials using example dimensions without measuring your own alcove and confirming the appliance-specific requirements.

hero.query: Shopping map for a hardware store in Seattle, organized aisles, natural light.

sections.scenario: Sneha shops a Seattle home center, then a hardware aisle, then a paint aisle — using the lumber-hardware-paint loop.
sections.principle: One loop: sheet goods, lumber, fasteners, then finish.
body: Walk once. Sheet goods and any shop cutting first. Then battens for cleats. Then screws, wall anchors matched to the substrate you identified, and sandpaper. Then primer, enamel, and mildew-resistant caulk. Home-center aisle maps and SKUs vary by store and region. Ask what the merchant will rip, what minimum strip width they will cut, and how you will get a 4 × 8 ft sheet into the elevator or up the stairs.

Carry the bill of materials and the smallest alcove width. Reject warped boards by sighting down the edge. If the shop cannot cut below a stated width, plan those rips at home with a guide, or change the design.
The later shopping chapters repeat this workflow with local store categories. Skip any US store name you still see in an old figure caption — the rule is the workflow, not the brand.
sections.mistake: Buying decorative brackets first and discovering you still have no sheet for the top.
checklist: Shop order written: sheets, lumber, fasteners, finish
Cutting limits asked before you pay

sections.title: Moisture-Safe Finishing Stack

hero.query: Moisture-safe finishing products for a laundry countertop, natural light, clean workspace.
hero.flux_prompt: A neatly arranged finishing station with primer and top coat products, emphasizing moisture protection.
hero.alt: A close-up of finishing products on a countertop.
hero.credit: Photo by Deane Bayas on Pexels

sections.principle: Seal every cut. Thin coats. Respect cure time — it can spill past Sunday.
body: Prime every raw edge and cut face. End grain on plywood drinks primer; give it a second coat. Then a satin or semi-gloss enamel that the label allows in a humid room. Caulk wall joints with a flexible, mildew-resistant product after primer and before or after the last paint coat as the caulk label directs.

Water-based products often recoat the same day; they still need the labeled dry time before you load wet laundry on the top. If the weekend ends before cure, that is a successful minimum-viable weekend: parts cut and sealed, installation postponed. Do not promise every finish stack in 48 hours.
Caulk and a drip pan protect surfaces. They are not a substitute for sound inlet hoses, reachable shutoffs, and a correctly placed drain hose.
sections.mistake: One thick enamel coat Saturday night, then stacking detergent bottles on a tacky film Sunday morning.
checklist: Labelled dry and cure times copied onto the schedule
MVP option written if cure overruns the weekend

sections.title: Span, Stiffness, And Load — Illustrative Only

hero.query: Countertop support structure for a 65-inch span, natural light, clean lines.
hero.flux_prompt: A detailed view of a countertop with support cleats and edge banding, showcasing structural integrity.
hero.alt: A close-up of the underside of a countertop showing support cleats.

sections.scenario: Karan’s Austin alcove is 65 inch between plasters. That number is his measurement, not a national standard.
sections.principle: Do not treat one span example as a universal design rule.
body: This book does not certify a maximum safe span for every plywood grade, every fastener, and every wall. State a span only as an example tied to a described stack. Example, not a rule: an 3/4 in plywood folding top, cleated on three sides into identified structure, with a front edge band, is a common way readers stiffen a roughly 1500–65 inch opening. If your opening is wider, your substrate is hollow plaster, or you only have two fasteners, this example does not apply.
Account for concentrated loads: a person leaning to fold, a full wet basket, someone sitting on the edge. If the top might be used as a seat or a step, stop — that is a different structure.

Add a center support or a shallow divider only when you have a wall, floor, or frame that can take that load without blocking hoses, vents, or machine removal. Recalculate after you measure. When in doubt, shorten the span or hire a carpenter who will stamp the method they use.

hero.query: Laundry alcove with measuring templates, one window light, linen textures, magazine styling, photorealistic.
hero.flux_prompt: Image of measuring templates laid out on a table with tools and materials.
hero.alt: Close-up of measuring tape against a wall.

sections.scenario: Priya’s Austin rental alcove, side-by-side compact machines, limited-fastener permission for two studs only if they exist — she will verify the substrate before drilling.
sections.principle: The governing width is the smallest of three; the governing depth is the shallowest of three.
body: Worked example (illustrative, then you replace every number). Width: 59 inch at the floor, 60 inch at mid-height, 59 inch at the top because of a trim lip. Governing width: 59 inch. Depth: 32 inch at center, 30 inch at the right because of trim. Governing depth: 30 inch. Height: 216 inch clear under the soffit. Washer: 27 inch wide, 82 in high, 27 inch deep cabinet, plus the hose bulge the manual names. Dryer beside it: same cabinet size. Door swing: 90 degrees, needs 2 in extra at the left casing.

Plumbing: shutoffs 16 inch left of center, 14 inch AFF (above finished floor). Drain standpipe behind the washer. Outlet on the right wall, keep a panel off it. No dryer duct — ventless dryer. Service path: both machines pull straight out 32 in. Those figures belong to this example. Yours come from your tape and your manuals.

How this turns into millwork: a folding top cannot be 59 inch if you need a scribe gap and you must not pinch the right-hand door. A rear cleat cannot cover the standpipe. Shelf depth starts from governing depth minus the maker’s rear clearance, not from a catalogue “24 inch” top. The cut-list chapter will show example parts for a similar width and will tell you to recalc.

sections.title: Fasteners Follow The Substrate

hero.query: Close-up of cleats and fasteners, one window light, plaster textures, magazine styling, photorealistic.
hero.flux_prompt: Image of cleats being installed on a wall with tools laid out.
hero.alt: Detailed view of a stud finder in use.
hero.credit: Photo by Los Muertos Crew on Pexels

sections.principle: A load-bearing wall is not automatically the right place for the fastener you have in the drawer.
body: Identify the wall before you drill. Concrete: masonry bits, suitable anchors, check for embedded services, respect landlord, HOA, or building drilling rules. Brick: do not explode a face brick for a heavy counter; use a method rated for that masonry and that load. Stud framing: fasten into suitable structural members you have located, not into the plaster skin. Drywall or hollow plaster only: hollow-wall anchors have low, orientation-dependent capacity — they are the wrong primary support for a loaded counter. Tile or wet finish: drilling can crack tile and admit water; stop if you cannot keep the hole sealed. Unknown substrate: stop and identify it.

Scribing means tracing the wall contour onto the panel and cutting to match. Shims are thin wedges that fill a gap so a cleat sits level. Service access means you can still reach hoses, vents, valves, and plugs after the millwork is in.
French cleats still need a substrate that can take the load. Two screws into hollow plaster are not a French-cleat system. If you cannot name the wall, you do not have a fastening plan.
sections.mistake: Hearing “load-bearing” and driving long screws without knowing whether the finish is 3/4 in plaster on brick or a hollow partition.
checklist: Fastener type matched to that substrate

sections.principle: A dry fit is cheaper than a second sheet.
body: Dry-fit the counter blank. Sand edges so they cannot cut skin or hoses. Pre-drill cleats. If walls bow, scribe, then reinstall. Screws into millwork should not replace the maker’s machine feet or shipping restraints.

Do not trap inlet hoses, drain hoses, or cords behind a fixed top you cannot lift without unscrewing a kitchen’s worth of hardware. A removable top or an access hatch next to the shutoffs is part of leak protection, not a luxury.
Organisation happens after the structure is stable and the machines can still come out. Bins do not fix a rocking cleat.
sections.mistake: Gluing a top down over the only shutoff access in the apartment.
checklist: Dry fit done on the governing width
Hoses and shutoffs reachable after the top is on
No sharp unsanded edges in the splash zone

sections.scenario: Ravi’s alcove is 34 inch wide with a bowed wall. He has a maker-approved stack kit for his exact washer and dryer models. Lease and HOA: no new exterior vent.
sections.principle: Stack only with an approved kit, and never on homemade millwork.
body: Typical combined stack height often lands near 1880–78 inch, but you must use the kit and both manuals. Confirm overhead clearance, service access to both units, and the removal path. A gas dryer, where one exists, adds fuel and combustion requirements — that is not a DIY vent-and-shelf problem.

In a rental, prefer no-drill or limited-fastener millwork beside the stack, not a platform the machines stand on unless that platform is designed for the load. Vibration pads belong only if the appliance maker allows them on that floor. Soft foam pads are the wrong answer for most washers.
Shelves beside a stack must not block lint access, controls, or the path to pull the pair. If the dryer is vented, the duct stays short, smooth, and cleanable — millwork does not pinch it.

sections.principle: Width, two door swings, and a folding top that does not carry the machines.
body: Full-size cabinets are often near 27–28 in wide each, but your two stickers win. Leave the side and rear clearances the manuals name. A folding top sits above the higher of the two tops plus the maker’s top clearance — not 1 inch because a blog said so.

A center divider under a folding top can make hamper lanes only if it does not block hoses or prevent pulling a machine. Fasten into identified structure. This is the permanent level: owner approval, and a carpenter or electrician if the wall or circuit is unclear.
Do not copy the 62 inch width onto someone else’s cut list. It is Anjali’s opening.

sections.principle: Sealed edges and a drip pan do not replace plumbing that can be shut off.
body: Prime every cut. Use materials from the moisture table. A drip pan is appropriate only where the appliance and floor allow it, and where you can still level the machine and reach a drain if the pan has one. Caulk is for splash. It is not a hidden-leak strategy behind a fixed panel.

Inlet hoses: inspect and replace on the interval the hose or machine maker names. Shutoff valves must stay reachable. Drain hoses must sit at the height the manual names, without kinks, unapproved extensions, or hanging unsecured.
After any move or reconnection, run a controlled short fill and watch joints before you leave the room. If you cannot see the connections because millwork hides them, the millwork is wrong.

If the wall is concrete or brick, the drill, the anchor, and the load all change. If you do not own the wall, limited-fastener work still needs permission and a patch plan.
Missing a stud in a framed wall is a reason to move the cleat or add a spreader that hits two members — not a reason to hang the same load from gypsum.

sections.principle: Do not move a washer or dryer alone with a towel and hope.
body: Read the appliance’s moving and transport instructions. Disconnect utilities using the proper procedure — water off, hoses drained, plug out, gas only by a qualified person. Secure drums and components as the maker requires (shipping bolts or transit bars on many washers). Use appropriate equipment and enough people for the mass of the machine. Protect flooring. Do not pinch hoses or cords. Reinstall, level, and reconnect per the manuals. Check for leaks and abnormal operation before normal use.

Cardboard is not a substitute for appliances sliders or a proper trolley when the machine is heavy or the floor is fragile. If you cannot recruit help or hire movers, postpone the pull-out and work around the machines.
Relevelling is not a coin trick. Follow the maker’s feet procedure. Then do a short controlled cycle.

steps.text: Read the moving section of the manual; refit shipping bolts if the maker requires them to tilt or transport.
Shut water, drain hoses, unplug; leave gas to a qualified person.
Move with enough people or equipment; never walk a full machine on its own feet across tile for sport.
Reinstall, level per the maker, then leak-check before a full load.

sections.principle: Four steps, in order. Skipping Verify is how shelves get built to the wrong wall.
body: Measure. Width at floor, mid, top. Depth at left, center, right. Height at back and front. Map outlet, hose box, standpipe, gas valve if any, and dryer vent or ventless clearance. Write inches. Do not round before tolerances.

Verify. Square the corners. Straightedge the bow. Copy service clearances from the manuals — including vent routing and whether a drip pan is appropriate. Confirm shipping bolts are out for use, and available if you must transport. Electrical: plug reachable, no extension-cord plan.

Decide. Use the appliance table from the opening chapter. Score access, storage, and stability only after front-load vs top-load vs stacked vs side-by-side vs washer-only is chosen. Stacked needs an approved kit. Side-by-side needs both door swings. Top-load needs lid height.
Sketch. Detergent reach, tall-bottle zone, folding surface that does not carry machines, hamper path, and a pull-out path. Mark cleats that must not cross a vent. Scribe notes where the wall bows.

Worked numbers (replace with yours): floor width 59 inch, mid 60 inch, top 59 inch — governing 59 inch. Depth 32 inch center, 30 inch right — governing 30 inch. Two compact 27 inch cabinets will not fit side-by-side in 59 inch once you add the maker’s side clearances and a door casing; this example therefore stacks with a factory kit and puts a 250–12 inch detergent shelf to the side, not over the exhaust path.

Dryer safety, dedicated: vented dryers need the maker’s duct, termination, and clearance; the path must not be blocked or casually flexible-hosed around a cleat; lint access stays cleanable. Ventless dryers still have clearances and lint. Gas dryers add fuel and combustion rules — qualified person. Do not assume the house has “a standard 4-inch vent.”

Plumbing as a system: inlet hose condition and replacement interval; shutoffs reachable; drain hose height and securing; no kinks or unapproved extensions; do not hide leaks behind a fixed top; drip pan only if it fits the appliance and floor; controlled leak check after reconnection. A pan plus caulk is not a plumbing install.

Anti-vibration: follow the maker’s leveling. Shipping bolts removed for operation, refitted for transport if required. Excess movement can be unbalanced load, uneven floor, bad leveling, or a machine fault — stop and investigate; do not keep stacking towels under feet. Rubber pads only if the maker and floor allow them. A coin on the lid is an informal observation, not proof of a correct install.
Pick the later cut-list variant only as a pattern: stacked-narrow, side-by-side, or compact side-by-side. Every dimension in those lists is illustrative.

sections.principle: Name what the envelope includes, then price locally.
body: Includes: plywood or other sheet goods, cleat lumber, screws and rated anchors, sandpaper, primer, paint, caulk, labels, and a small drip pan if you use one. Excludes: washer, dryer, stacking kit, plumber, electrician, appliance delivery, and tools you own. Prices move by city; treat the envelope as a shopping cap, not a quote.

If a merchant’s 3/4 in plywood sheet alone blows half the envelope, reduce shelf count, skip decorative trim, or postpone the project. Do not “save” money with untreated particle board in the splash zone.
Standard US sheet goods are 4 × 8 ft. If you shop outside the United States, convert the $200 envelope and check local sheet sizes.

Cleats: 1x2 or 1x3 battens, or plywood strips. Confirm actual dressed sizes at the shop — Confirm dressed 1×3 size at the rack — it is not a full 1 inch by 3 inches.
Fasteners: buy what the substrate table named. Do not buy a random metal bracket set that only hits plaster.
Finish: bonding primer, washable enamel, mildew-resistant flexible caulk. Edge band is optional; paint is not optional on raw edges.

sections.principle: Every length below is a pattern. Recalculate after you measure.
body: Do not cut materials using example dimensions without measuring your own alcove and confirming the appliance-specific requirements. Example lists assume inches, a folding top that does not carry machines, and clearances still matching the manuals after the parts go in. They do not automatically include your wall bow, your baseboard, or your sheet thickness.

Three patterns. Side-by-side: a full folding top, rear and side cleats, optional short uprights — only if width after clearances allows both doors. Stacked-narrow: a cleat ladder beside the stack, shelves, a small side ledge — only with an approved stack kit. Compact side-by-side: a shorter top and a center support if, and only if, that support has somewhere honest to land and does not block hoses.

Starting sizes to adjust, not to copy: folding top depth often 24–25 in so hoses behind the machines still breathe — verify against cabinet depth plus rear clearance. Shelf depth 250–12 inch for bottles. Vertical gaps 350–16 inch for tall bottles, 250–12 inch for baskets. Cleats long enough to hit two structural points when you are on the limited-fastener or permanent level.

Example A, illustrative, side-by-side pattern, 161 inch opening, 3/4 in plywood: top 1600 × 27 inch (scribe gap left). Shelves 1600 × 12 inch. Rear cleats 59 inch. This is not your cut list if your governing width is 59 inch or your manual forbids that depth.
Example B, illustrative, stacked pattern, 32 inch opening: three shelves 780 × 12 inch and a 500 × 27 inch side ledge. Recalc if the stack kit needs different side clearance.
Example C, illustrative, compact side-by-side, 52 in opening: top 51 × 24 in plus a center support only on identified structure.

Edges: paint, iron-on band, or a timber lip. Jig: straightedge plus a spacer block. Labels on the hidden face: CT, SH1, RC. Pre-drill. Leave a scribe gap. Span at least two honest structure points for a loaded cleat. Sparse drywall screws are not a system.
Counter height: above the higher machine plus the maker’s top clearance. Many front-load cabinets are near 38–40 in high; your sticker wins. Never drop a top onto a top-load lid arc.

sections.scenario: Mia’s Austin alcove is 30 inch. Lease: no wall drilling.
sections.principle: If the wall cannot be used, the floor and a designed frame must do the work — or you scale down.
body: No-drill means freestanding or fully removable parts that do not rely on wall attachment. A homemade 2×4 platform under stacked machines is not automatically safe: it changes height, drain geometry, and load. Do not build a machine plinth unless it is designed for that mass and the maker still allows the installation.
Vibration pads only if the maker allows them. A drip pan only if it fits and you can still level. Do not block hose paths.

If no-drill cannot hold your shelves without tipping, drop to bins on the machines (where the maker allows) or negotiate limited fasteners. Do not tension a post into a concrete ceiling until you know the finish can take it.

steps.text: Write “no-drill” on the sheet only if zero wall screws are required.
Reject homemade machine plinths unless designed for the load.
Keep hose and drain geometry identical to the manuals.

sections.title: Press-Fit Frames Have Limits

sections.principle: Friction against paint is not a verified load rating.
body: A press-fit upright is a post cut slightly long and compressed between floor and ceiling with pads. Damage: crushed plaster, cracked POP, marked paint. Load: treat as light shelves only unless an engineer or carpenter rates it. Permission: still ask; ceiling damage counts. Removal: relieve pressure slowly so the finish does not pop. Stability during removal: brace before you knock the post out.
Over-tensioning can damage the ceiling. Stop when the post is firm, not when the slab sings. Do not use this to carry a dryer.
If the washer walks, the frame must not become a lever on the ceiling. Stop and investigate the machine first.
sections.mistake: Calling a compressed 2×4 renter-friendly because it “comes out,” after it spider-cracks the POP.

sections.principle: A French cleat is only as honest as the wall behind it.
body: Limited-fastener: landlord permission, substrate identified, load matched, patch plan. A French cleat (two 45-degree interlocking strips) can hang a shallow shelf if the wall piece hits real structure. Two screws in hollow plaster are not enough for a loaded detergent shelf.
Test with a known light load first. Keep the shelf shallow. Do not hang it over a spinning washer unless the wall and cleat are rated for vibration plus mass.
Photograph hole locations for move-out. Permission in writing beats a verbal “it’s fine.”

Drip pan lip cannot lift the machine past what the drain hose and the maker allow.
If the frame shakes with the spin, stop. Do not add a diagonal that ties a walking machine to a weak ceiling.

Pocket screws belong in millwork joints, not as a way to grab empty plaster.
If you cannot find structure, hire a carpenter. Vibration from a washer will announce a bad anchor at 2 a.m.

Trim must not become a lip that traps water against raw board.

Humidity in monsoon months extends dry time. The schedule chapter expects that.

hero.query: A well-protected laundry alcove with a drip pan, splash guard, and smooth aluminum duct, emphasizing functionality and cleanliness.

sections.principle: Millwork sits around services. It does not replace them.
body: Plumbing system: inlet hose age and maker replacement interval; shutoffs reachable with the top in place; drain hose height, securing, no kinks, no casual extra length; leak inspection after moving; drip pan only if appropriate. Do not hide the hose box behind a fixed panel.

Dryer: vented vs ventless. Vented — follow the maker’s duct, termination, and clearance; keep lint cleanable; do not crush or endlessly flex-duct around shelves. Gas dryer — qualified person for fuel and combustion. Ventless — still respect clearances and lint.

Electrical: requirements from the rating plate; keep the plug inspectable; no unsuitable extension cords; no overloaded adaptors; electrician for modifications. This book does not give a generic inch clearance to an outlet for every code. If water and electricity share the alcove, the arrangement must satisfy applicable electrical safety rules — when unsure, stop.
sections.mistake: A smooth painted box covering the shutoff, the lint path, and a dangling adaptor.

body: Dry-fit, trace, cut toward the line, refit. Shims behind cleats can level a low spot; a thick shim stack is a spongy shelf. If the alcove is badly out of square, reduce depth so the part floats clear, then trim.

sections.principle: Every millwork part points at one governing measurement.
body: Copy this worked example, then replace it. Alcove plan: 59 inch governing width, 30 inch governing depth, 216 inch height. Widths: 1500 / 1525 / 59 inch (floor, mid, top). Depths: 32 inch left, 32 inch center, 30 inch right (trim). Appliance: stacked front-load pair on a factory kit; cabinet 27 inch wide; follow the kit’s height. Door: front-load swing 90 degrees, keep 2 in to the left casing. Plumbing: shutoffs 16 inch left of center at 14 inch AFF; standpipe behind. Outlet: right wall, keep a 12 in keep-out so a panel cannot cover the plug — that keep-out is a layout habit, not a code number. Vent: none (ventless). Labels: Cleat A at 36 inch AFF for a side ledge if the kit allows; Cleat B at 56 inch AFF for detergent — both heights are examples and must clear the dryer door and lint path.

Which number governs what. Uprights and top length: 59 inch minus scribe minus any required side clearance. Shelf depth: 30 inch minus rear clearance minus any door clash. Side ledge depth: bottle height and elbow room, not the full cabinet depth. Cleat lengths: structure spacing, not the full plaster width if that would cover the standpipe.
Conversion: 25 mm is about 1 inch. Use inches on the cut list. Do not mix millimetres into an inch sheet. Photograph the labeled alcove.
Incomplete sentences belong in the bin. If a template line has no number, it is not measured.

body: At Menards, start in the yard or rear saw for panels and studs. Measure and record the sizes you need. Protect edges for the ride home.
Use the long hardware run for screws and anchors. Check length against your actual thickness.
Paint counter for bonding primer and washable enamel. If the label needs overnight between coats, Sunday install may wait.

steps.text: Stage panels with edge protection before you leave the yard.
Match screw length to board thickness plus cleat.
Put recoat time on the weekend schedule.

sections.scenario: Ravi and Priya cap millwork at $200 in their Austin one-bedroom. Machines are already paid for.
sections.principle: The checklist keeps millwork inside the envelope and inside the manuals.
body: Use this list to reduce decision fatigue, not to force a 48-hour miracle. Core success is machines that still open, drain, and sit still, plus millwork that does not fight them.
Budget line: millwork ≤ $200 unless you consciously raise it. Still excludes trades and appliances.
If you fall behind, keep path lighting for the wet floor, reachable shutoffs, and a working washer. Drop the fourth shelf.

sections.principle: A checkpoint is permission to continue — or to stop.
body: Print the list. Mark boxes. At each checkpoint ask: is it safe and appropriate to continue? If the wall is unknown, if the stack kit is missing, if the enamel is wet, the answer is no.
Cross-reference earlier chapters instead of rewriting them on the wall.
Keep one marker color for inches and another for notes so units do not mix.

sections.principle: Empty, measure, photograph, decide.
body: Clear the alcove or pull machines with the safe procedure. Measure. Note outlets and hoses. Review the cut-list pattern you will recalc. If walls are glossy, primer time belongs on Saturday’s clock.
Confirm help for any lift. Confirm landlord permission if you are not at the no-drill level.
If you cannot finish Friday prep, do not buy irreversible sheets on Saturday morning.

sections.principle: Do not use the finished alcove until the inspection passes.
body: Shop the local loop. Verify boards against the recalc cut list. Straight stock only. If a size is missing, change the list, not the safety margins.

Final inspection, before normal use: appliance clearances and full door or lid operation; counter and shelves stable under a realistic lean and a full basket (not a person standing on them); fasteners and supports tight on the structure you named; water shutoffs and drain reachable; electrical plug accessible, no unsuitable cords; no blocked vents, lint paths, or service access; no sharp exposed edges; finishes and sealants cured as labeled; controlled leak check after reconnection; a clear removal or service path for the machines.
If any line fails, the alcove is not finished. Use the machines in their safe prior state until it passes. That is the last practical step of this book.

steps.text: Buy only after the cut list uses your inches.
Install only at the construction level you chose.
Run the full final inspection; fail any blocked service or leak.
